q: Out of the following, what is true about the fundamental rights?
options: They are basic and inalienable human rights
They are not limited by the Constitution
They are absolute and not amenable to change
They are granted by the Constitution
key_text: They are granted by the Constitution
explanation: FRs are granted (guaranteed) by the Constitution. They are limited by reasonable restrictions and amendable, so 'not limited' and 'absolute' are wrong.

notes.text: - **Right:** "not absolute", "some only for citizens", "drawn from the American Constitution", "justiciable", "six in number", "granted by the Constitution".
- **Wrong:** "FRs are **unamendable**", "**absolute**", "partly justiciable and absolute", "not limited by the Constitution", "all FRs are suspended in an emergency".

q: Fundamental rights are claimed mostly against
explanation: FRs are claims mostly against the State; they limit the power of the State, even Parliament.

notes.text: - **Claimed against the State:** most FRs are available against **arbitrary State action** and **limit the power of the State – even Parliament**; some (15(2), 17, 23, 24) also bind private persons.

q: A proclamation of National Emergency automatically suspends
explanation: Under Art. 358, a National Emergency (war/external aggression) automatically suspends Art. 19, the Right to Freedom; other FRs need a Presidential order under Art. 359, and Arts. 20-21 are never suspended.

notes.text: - **Art. 358:** when a National Emergency is declared on **war or external aggression**, **Art. 19 (Right to Freedom) is suspended automatically** (not on armed rebellion).

q: One among the following is authorized to impose restrictions of Fundamental Rights:
explanation: Reasonable restrictions on FRs are imposed by law made by the legislature – Parliament – not by the President or Prime Minister (the President only suspends enforcement during an emergency). (Printed key President corrected.)

notes.text: - **Reasonable restrictions** are imposed by **law** made by **Parliament** (and State legislatures within their field) – not by the President, Prime Minister or Supreme Court; the courts only **judge** their reasonableness.

q: Under Which Article of the Constitution of India can the Fundamental Rights of the members of the Armed forces be specifically restricted
explanation: Art. 33 lets Parliament restrict the FRs of the armed forces; Arts. 19, 21 and 25 are rights, not restricting powers.

q: Fundamental freedoms recognised by Constitution of India
explanation: Article 19 now recognises six fundamental freedoms; the seventh, property, was deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978) – already the position in 2012.

notes.text: - **Article 19** guarantees **six freedoms** to citizens (not Arts. 14, 18, 20, 21 or 22) – **seven originally** (asked as "seven freedoms" in older papers); the 7th, property, was deleted.

q: Under which Article of the Constitution citizens are granted seven freedoms?
explanation:
the "seven freedoms" were cut to six by the 44th Amendment, 1978 — now Article 19 grants six freedoms (Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978)
Article 19 originally granted seven freedoms (now six). (now six: 19(1)(f) property was deleted in 1978)

notes.text: - **Article 19** guarantees **six freedoms** to citizens (not Arts. 14, 18, 20, 21 or 22) – **seven originally** (asked as "seven freedoms" in older papers); the 7th, property, was deleted.

q: Freedom of profession, occupation or trade is protected by Article ..... of India constitution
explanation: Freedom of profession, occupation, trade or business is Article 19(1)(g).

q: Which one among the following is not guaranteed by the Constitution of India as a fundamental right?
options: Freedom to move freely throughout the country
Freedom to assemble peacefully without arms
Freedom to own, acquire and dispose a property anywhere in the country
Freedom to practice any trade or profession
key_text: Freedom to own, acquire and dispose a property anywhere in the country
explanation: The freedom to own, acquire and dispose of property is no longer a Fundamental Right; 19(1)(f) was deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978).

notes.text: - **Not in Article 19(1):** **equal opportunity** (Art. 16), **property** (deleted 1978), **moving out of the country** (travel abroad = **Art. 21**, Maneka Gandhi 1978), **freedom of conscience** (Art. 25).
- **Property** was removed as a Fundamental Right by the **44th Amendment Act, 1978** (now Art. 300A, a legal right).

q: Which Article of the Constitution prescribes six freedoms?
explanation: Article 19 prescribes the six freedoms; Arts. 18, 20 and 21 deal with titles, conviction and life/liberty.

notes.text: - **Article 19** guarantees **six freedoms** to citizens (not Arts. 14, 18, 20, 21 or 22) – **seven originally** (asked as "seven freedoms" in older papers); the 7th, property, was deleted.
